segments.caption: Roll one dice, and every number is equally likely. The shape is flat.
Now roll ten dice and take their average. Again, and again.
The averages make a bell!
That's the Central Limit Theorem.
Take many samples, and find the mean of each one.
Plot those means, and they form a normal distribution.
Even when the original data isn't normal at all.
One dice is flat.
The average of two dice? A triangle, peaking at 3.5.
Five dice? Rounder.
Thirty dice? A clean bell, centred on 3.5.
It works for skewed data too.
Waiting times at a bus stop have a long tail to the right.
But the averages of thirty waiting times? A bell again.
The bell is centred on the true mean.
And bigger samples make it narrower.
Its spread is the standard deviation, divided by the square root of n.
That's called the standard error.
That's why the normal distribution shows up everywhere.
It's how polls get their margin of error, and how scientists test if a result is real.
How big is big enough? A common rule of thumb is 30.
Very skewed data may need more.
Here's the complete picture.
Take many samples, and plot their means.
They form a bell around the true mean, whatever the original shape.
And bigger samples make that bell narrower.
Quick quiz!
Heights have a standard deviation of 7 centimetres. You average samples of 49 people.
What's the spread of those averages?
1 centimetre!
7, divided by the square root of 49, which is 7, gives 1.
In future videos, we'll explore other kinds of distributions.
